comparison: Perfect agreement on foundational claims (C1, C2, C3, C9, C10) about working memory function and study motivation. Both evaluations find these well-supported by established literature.

Strong agreement on experimental design quality (C4, C5, C11, C12, C13). OpenEval provides more technical detail on sample size and eye-tracking methodology, while peer reviewers emphasize the innovative orthogonalization as 'clever' and 'noteworthy.'
Perfect agreement on behavioral performance data (C14, C15). Both accept that participants performed above chance, validating the task paradigm. Peer reviewers do not question these basic metrics.

Perfect agreement on past location bias findings (C17, C18, C19, C49). Both evaluations find strong statistical support (p<0.001) and acknowledge this replicates prior work. Peer reviewers explicitly note the 'fairly clear' evidence in Figure 1b-d.

Strong agreement on future location bias as novel finding (C20, C21, C50). Both evaluations emphasize the novelty and statistical significance. Peer reviewers describe the 'ramping up' pattern and call the observation 'noteworthy.'

Strong agreement on single-saccade analysis demonstrating joint consideration (C28-C34, with C22 overlap). Both find this evidence 'compelling' and 'persuasive.' OpenEval emphasizes the statistical interaction, while peer reviewers highlight the dependency pattern in Figure 2 as definitive evidence.

Strong agreement on the primary conclusion of simultaneous retention (C6, C7, C8, C35, C41, C43). Both evaluations affirm this as the central contribution. Peer reviewers call it 'important' and note it 'advances our understanding,' while OpenEval emphasizes converging evidence from multiple analyses.

Perfect agreement on theoretical interpretation (C36, C37) regarding future orientation and retention of past attributes. Both accept this interpretation without challenge, with peer reviewers acknowledging the plausibility of the theoretical accounts.

Perfect agreement on remapping hypothesis rejection (C38, C39, C40). Both evaluations accept the analysis and interpretation. Peer reviewers do not challenge the evidence against pure remapping accounts.

Agreement on microsaccade-driven effects and temporal dynamics (C23, C24). OpenEval addresses consistency across trial types, while peer reviewers accept the temporal characterizations including the early peak and ramping patterns without challenge.

Agreement on temporal dynamics (C25, C26). OpenEval emphasizes differential time courses suggesting distinct functional roles, while peer reviewers accept the temporal patterns described (early peak vs. ramping) without question.

Strong agreement on methodological advantages of microsaccades (C46, C47, C48). Both evaluations praise the approach as 'state-of-the-art' and 'compelling,' with peer reviewers emphasizing fine temporal resolution and the editor noting it builds on the authors' recent work.

Strong agreement on content-specificity argument (C52, C53, C54, C56, C57). Both find the logical inference from the experimental design sound. Peer reviewers accept the orthogonalization as a key design feature distinguishing this from pre-cue studies.

Agreement on speculative interpretations (C58, C59, C60, C61, C64). OpenEval explicitly labels these as 'UNCERTAIN' and appropriately speculative, while peer reviewers accept them as reasonable possibilities without challenge, noting they are presented as interpretive rather than definitive.

OpenEval finds the contextualization within broader literature (C62, C63) well-supported with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these specific claims about allocentric/egocentric frame parallels.

Partial overlap on novelty claims (C16, C42, C43). OpenEval distinguishes expected findings from novel contributions, while peer reviewers focus on C43 as part of the central contribution. Both affirm the advance beyond existing knowledge.

OpenEval evaluates sample size justification and participant replacement (C65, C66) as appropriate methodological practice, though notes power calculation could be more formal. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these methodological details.
